props.title: Poetry
props.initialSlug: Elderly woman finds poetry amid tragedy and dementia

sections.content: **Poetry** (2010) stands as one of Korean director Lee Chang-dong's most devastating masterpieces. The film follows Mija, an elderly woman facing early dementia while taking a poetry class, who discovers her grandson's involvement in a horrific crime. Like Lee's Secret Sunshine (2007) and Burning (2018), Poetry weaponizes slow-burning tension to explore profound moral questions. The film's power lies in veteran actress Yoon Jeong-hee's heartbreaking performance - her last role before retiring - capturing both gentle curiosity and mounting despair as Mija processes unthinkable truths.

sections.content: Poetry connects thematically to other powerful Asian films examining elderly women facing moral and existential crises. **The Truth** (2019) by Hirokazu Kore-eda explores an aging actress confronting family tensions, while Hong Sang-soo's **On the Beach at Night Alone** (2017) uses poetic structure to probe personal guilt. These films share Poetry's contemplative pacing and focus on female characters wrestling with societal expectations and personal accountability.

The film's examination of memory and creativity parallels works like Still Alice (2014) and **Iris** (2001), though Lee Chang-dong avoids their more conventional approaches to depicting cognitive decline. Instead, Poetry's power comes from showing how art and moral awakening can emerge even as mental faculties fade. The poetry classes Mija attends become both escape and confrontation - each lesson forcing her to "really look" at the world while she grapples with mounting horror. SUBHEAD: Korean New Wave Context

sections.content: Poetry emerged during a crucial period in Korean cinema, alongside works like Mother (2009) and **I Wish I Knew** (2010) that challenged conventional narrative structures. Lee Chang-dong's background as a novelist informs the film's literary sensibility, while his experience as South Korea's Minister of Culture adds depth to its social commentary. The film's precise composition and patient storytelling exemplify the sophisticated craftsmanship that helped Korean cinema gain international recognition years before **Parasite** (2019) broke through to mainstream success.
